body:
This week’s challenge wasn’t in finding Torah to speak about—quite the opposite. There was too much to say. So many ideas, but the delivery felt stuck. And maybe that’s exactly the point: the how of the message depends deeply on the who that is delivering it. Every message must come through the prism of the self. And that’s why this parsha strikes such a chord.

Noach’s Individual Tafkid Noach is called a tzaddik in his generation (Bereishis 6:9). He walked with Hashem. That’s not a side note—it’s a profound identity. But he didn’t do outreach like Avraham. He built the teivah, saved his family, and followed Hashem’s word precisely (Rashi ad loc). That was his avodah. We often focus on what he didn’t do—but what he did do requires enormous strength.

Noach lived in a time of total corruption (Bereishis 6:11). The world had become immoral to the point that even the animals had been influenced (Rashi, Bereishis 6:12). In such a time, Noach’s righteousness was not a passive quality. It was built through boundaries. He created space between himself and the outside. He didn’t absorb the world; he protected his teivah. He may not have brought others in, but he preserved what mattered.

And when people asked him what he was building, he told them and he told them why. He wasn’t silent, he didn’t compromise, and he didn’t lower the message (Sanhedrin 108b). He just didn't go out to tell people the message—he told it to them when they came to him.

The Animal World and Its Reflections Even within the teivah, the avodah was demanding. Noach cared for the animals, but even there, it wasn’t smooth. One time he was late feeding the lion, and the lion bit him (Sanhedrin 108b). We see that even the act of kindness, of duty, can carry risk. Lions are powerful, social animals. Whether it was just a reminder bite or a reflection of a group pack animal on someone who was quiet, there is a lot to learn even from this.

Then, when it came time to re-engage the world, Noach sent out the raven first (Bereishis 8:7). The raven didn’t fulfill the mission. Rashi explains that the raven circled, suspicious that Noach had ulterior motives (Rashi, Bereishis 8:7). But the Gemara in Pesachim 113b hints to us something else: that ravens are among those species that love their own kind.

This is striking. The raven may not have succeeded in this task, but it is a creature of connection and loyalty. Its failure may not be due to selfishness, but rather to a kind of insularity. The raven operates in community. But community alone isn’t always sufficient—sometimes it may only respond to a community.

Later, ravens find their moment. In the days of Eliyahu HaNavi, it is the raven that feeds him (Melachim I 17:4–6). It brings food to the prophet who was in hiding, rejected by society, preserving truth from within. The raven didn't help Noach, but it helped Eliyahu. In the right context, its koach became invaluable.

The Dove and Its Simplicity The dove, on the other hand, fulfills its task (Bereishis 8:11). It flies out, returns with the olive branch. Doves are quiet, personal birds. They don’t nest communally. They aren’t loud. They live simple lives.

And later, we see doves brought as korbanos—for the poor, the recovering mother, the baal teshuva (Vayikra 1:14, 12:8, 14:22). They are korbanos of individuals. Not for the tzibbur. Not for grandeur. The dove speaks to the person who needs something gentle, private, restorative.

In a sense, the raven and the dove represent two modes of mission. The raven, bound by group loyalty, couldn’t reach outward at first. But later, its communal koach served a navi. The dove, by contrast, represents the private healing of the individual.

And here lies a subtle but profound contrast: the raven was not able to respond to the internal, individualized tzaddik like Noach. It needed the external navi—Eliyahu—or perhaps someone like Avraham, to fulfill its purpose. The raven’s strength is communal, activated best in service of those who operate outwards.

But the dove—precisely because of its quiet, personal nature—could respond to Noach. It understood the language of inner worlds. The dove was able to return to the teivah because Noach’s avodah matched its essence: inward, simple, steady.

In this contrast we learn something about ourselves too. Some missions respond only to the one who goes out. Others awaken when met by stillness and depth within. And each is holy in its time.

From Noach to Avraham: A Generational Shift After the mabul, the world rebuilds. But then we see the Tower of Bavel, a massive collective project, but one without proper spiritual grounding (Bereishis 11:4). Mass cooperation aimed in the wrong direction. That’s the shadow side of unity without purpose.

At this point, Avram arises. He is not yet Avraham Avinu, but he already begins to step out. His koach is outreach. He teaches. He spreads the name of Hashem (Bereishis 12:5; Rashi). This is a different tafkid than Noach’s—and it is needed now. And yet, we should note: Noach and Avram overlapped for 57 years (Seder Olam Rabbah ch. 1). The transition was not immediate. Both roles coexisted.

Sometimes the world needs a Noach. Sometimes an Avram. And sometimes both.

How do we prepare ourselves for the world and the water? The mabul water was boiling and acidic, Chazal say it was laced with destructive forces (Rashi, Bereishis 7:23; Sanhedrin 108b). But we also say ein mayim ela Torah (Bava Kamma 17a). Water can destroy, or it can nurture. The same substance, depending on direction.

In the Kuzari (Maamar 3), the Chaver explains that each Jew is like a limb in the body. When connected, the body thrives. When disconnected, the limb is lost. This is true in tefillah, in learning, in communal mission. When we unite b’derech tov, the waters are redemptive.

Mar Cheshvan and the Ten-Day Window The Mabul began on the 17th of Mar Cheshvan (Rashi, Bereishis 7:11). In Eretz Yisrael, we begin davening for rain on the 7th, ten days earlier.

An opportunity to of ten days of preparation, of bracha-seeking before the memory of destruction. Ten days, like Aseres Yemei Teshuva. Like the Ten Utterances. Like the Ten Middos of Hashem.

We are reminded: water is coming. Will it be a mabul or a mikvah?

Sitting at the Feet of Tzaddikim There’s a powerful model that runs through this entire parsha: sitting at the feet of tzaddikim. Chazal teach us to "be covered in the dust of their feet" (Avos 1:4)—to draw near to those who walk the path of truth, even if their styles differ. Noach, Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov—each one had a different expression of greatness. And each of them offers something for us. We don’t have to become them, but we can draw from them. Learn from their kochos. Reflect their light. Sometimes we learn to set boundaries; sometimes to tear them down. Sometimes to hold firm; sometimes to reach outward. We don’t follow blindly—we learn with discernment. And through that, we grow.

Final Reflections We are not Noach. We are not Avraham. But we carry something from both. There are times we need to retreat and preserve. There are times we need to step out and speak. The key is to discern which tafkid is ours today. And to never forget that even within what looks like inaction, there may be deep avodah taking place.

May we be zocheh to recognize our individual tafkid, to honor the different voices within our mesorah, and to draw down water that heals and nourishes, not water that floods and burns.

Gut Shabbos.
